name: Chrome Carnival
description: A three-day street festival originating in Tier 2's Mwangi-Szczepański Corridor celebrating augmentation culture — not the corporate-sanitized version, but the self-modified, jury-rigged, aesthetically chaotic chrome of working-class cyberware. Participants display their augmentations openly, and 'chrome walks' (informal parades of the heavily modified) wind through the district. The festival was founded by a collective of augmentation artists who rejected the Tier 4 'precision chrome' aesthetic in favor of visible seams, mixed hardware, and deliberate asymmetry.
cultural_impact: Chrome Carnival has gradually shifted public perception of working-class augmentation from 'necessity modification' to a recognized aesthetic tradition with its own critics, historians, and stars. Corporate augmentation brands have begun attempting to market 'authentic imperfection' lines, which are widely mocked at the festival itself.
key_figures: The Patchwork Saints (chrome walk performance collective)
Roshan Yıldız-Nkemdirim (underground augmentation tech, festival medic)
story_hooks: A corporate augmentation brand has hired an infiltrator to 'discover' and photograph specific festival participants for an unauthorized ad campaign — the infiltrator is having second thoughts after three days among the Corridor community.

This year's chrome walk route passes directly through a block that Helix Infrastructure Corp has quietly purchased and plans to demolish — the festival may be the last time anyone walks those streets.

A chrome walk participant collapses mid-parade, their jury-rigged spinal augmentation failing catastrophically. The festival medic stabilizes them but discovers the hardware failure was not accidental — someone tampered with it.
origin_event: A 2211 open-air exhibition organized by Celestine Adeyemi-Kowalski in response to a Tier 4 augmentation magazine that described Shelf chrome as 'functional deformity,' which drew 400 participants and became an annual tradition.
tier_observations: Tier 1 residents come to the Corridor for the chrome walks and the Solder Market, trading parts and getting informal augmentation work done. Tier 2 workers are the core participants — this is their festival. Tier 3 attendees come as observers and increasingly as enthusiastic participants, often getting criticized for 'chrome tourism.' Tier 4 residents occasionally attend in disguise or watch streaming feeds, some genuinely moved and some condescending. Tier 5 is entirely absent except for corporate intelligence gatherers.
